highlights.text: a single core sense: seeking after / going in quest of something (ibtighāʾ)
ṭalaba / yaṭlubu / ṭalab — to seek a thing
Dhū al-Rummah: two Kalbī shepherds lost their charge after turning back from a muṭlib
Two roots:
badartu ilā al-shayʾi / bādartu — to hasten toward something
a line of poetry by Kuthayyir about passion and rushing tears
something perishing or coming to ruin
bāda al-shayʾu baydan wa-buyūdan
We are the last [nation], [yet] the foremost on the Day of Resurrection — bayda (however) that they [earlier nations] were given the Book before us
two sound origins: (1) splitting/cleaving, and (2) winning and endurance
Winning and endurance (fawz wa baqāʾ), yielding الفَلَاح (falāḥ)
الْحَدِيدُ بِالْحَدِيدِ يُفْلَحُ ("iron is cleaved by iron")
A ḥadīth uses it in this sense: they prayed with the Prophet until they feared missing al-falāḥ (the pre-dawn meal).
a single core sense: stealthy seizure or destruction
ghālahu yaghūluhu — "it took/destroyed him from where he did not perceive [it]."
an unattributed line of verse picturing a riding-mount stretching out over such remote distance
jumud, the solidifying or congealing of something that was liquid
jamada al-ma'u yajmudu, "the water froze/solidified."
al-Mutalammis uses the contrast directly
taking or carrying off a thing wholesale — sweeping the whole of it away at once
a bank or stretch of ground that a flash-flood (sayl) eats away/erodes
ease in flowing, or in running, or otherwise
A line of poetry by al-Namir is cited using "ghayr maʿn"
one sound root whose core idea is contempt and lowness
مَهِين (mahīn) means حَقِير — contemptible, paltry.
a sound root with three meanings: a kind of sound, roughness in a thing
makā yamkū, verbal noun mukāʾ, is to whistle into one's hand held gathered together
ʿAntara uses it of a spear-wound
derives the root ن-ح-ب (n-ḥ-b) from two basic senses
al-naḥb (النَّحْب) = "the vow" (al-nadhr)
One core meaning: a kind of sound, from which further senses branch.
shajarah nakhirah (a decayed tree) and ʿaẓm nakhir (a decayed bone) belong to the same root
a line/mark, writing, and anything resembling these
al-raqīm = "the writing" / an inscription.
"he inscribes upon water" (yarqumu fī l-māʾ), said of someone extremely skilled at his craft
the idea of becoming firm and fixed (thabata)
"lofty rawāsī" (Q 77:27): firmly fixed mountains.
"and the mountains, He set them firm (arsāhā)" (Q 79:32).
A poet: "and there are no mountains when the pegs do not hold firm."
good and joy, the opposite of ill-omen (naḥs)
al-saʿd — good fortune in a matter
source of the proverb "no pasture like al-saʿdān."
a single core idea with two branches: (a) letting something down from a high place to a low one, and (b) something extending or stretching out
السَّبِيل (al-sabīl) = the road or way, so named because it stretches out
a single core idea: following / succession (al-ittibāʿ)
تِلَاوَة for reciting the Qurʼān, because the reciter takes one verse after another in sequence
a line of Ibn Muqbil on "the remnants of youth" now gone without sight or trace
a single organizing sense: al-tark, "leaving off / relinquishing a thing."
a deceased person's estate: what he leaves behind of his inheritance (turāth)
He cites al-Aʿshā: in a trackless desert one finds ostrich eggs left abandoned
does not reduce to one governing idea (qiyās); its senses are separate
Al-witr / al-watar — the single, odd, unpaired one (opposite of paired/even).
"wataartuhu" means "I wronged/deprived him [of a kinsman]
a core sense of trusting/relying and, correspondingly, of binding firmly
al-mīthāq — a compact confirmed by an oath and covenant
al-Fajr 89:26 ("none binds as He binds")
feminine of al-awthaq, "the firmest / most reliable."
a single root meaning to lower or abase oneself (taṭāmun)
to lower oneself and bow the head
Poetic shāhid (Jarīr): at the news of al-Zubayr's death, "the walls of the city and the humbled mountains sank low."
roughness and coarseness/thickness — one single underlying sense according to Ibn Fāris
he takes all of the above to be derived from al-khashab, "wood/timber."
a hadith about Mecca: "It will not perish until its two akhshabs perish," meaning the two mountains [flanking the city]
"wakefulness, alertness."
النوم "sleep" vs. اليقظة "wakefulness."
plural ayqāẓ = "a wakeful group."
Shāhid from al-Farazdaq (satirical verse): "They wake at their donkeys' braying ...
derives the root ز-م-ل (z-m-l) from two distinct original senses
"wraps himself up" (تَزَمَّلَ, tazammala) — piling on garments until he resembles a bundled load
a line by the poet Uḥayḥah mocking a "lazy zummayl"
a single core idea: the pairing or bringing-together of one thing alongside another
the woman in turn is the zawj (spouse) of her mate
each member of a matched pair is a zawj
a man "has two zawj-s of pigeons," meaning one male and one female
he reports the view that zawj here means color ("of every splendid color")
